notes.b: Sugars are the sweet, water-loving carbohydrates, and these two properties explain why they are used so widely in cooking. Starch is the contrast: it is neither sweet nor soluble in cold water.
points: All sugars are sweet, but to different degrees. Fructose is sweeter than sucrose (table sugar), and lactose (milk sugar) is the least sweet of the common sugars.
On a scale where sucrose scores 100, the 2017 marking scheme gives fructose 170 and lactose 15. Learn the order (fructose, then sucrose, then lactose) and use the figures only as that scale.
Sweetness is why sugar is used to sweeten cakes, desserts, drinks and sweets.
Sugars are white crystalline solids that dissolve readily in water, and solubility increases with temperature, so more sugar dissolves in hot water than in cold.
A concentrated sugar solution is a syrup. Syrups are used to sweeten drinks and sauces, to make icing and to bottle fruit.
Starch is different: it is insoluble in cold water, so it does not dissolve but settles as a cloudy suspension (tiny solid particles spread through the liquid). It is also not sweet.
notes.tip: Do not mix up soluble (dissolves) with hygroscopic (absorbs water from the air). Starch fails the first test in cold water but passes the second.

notes.b: Starch behaves differently from sugar: it is insoluble in cold water and must be heated with a liquid before it thickens anything. It also takes in moisture from the air.
points: Gelatinisation: when starch is heated in a liquid, the granules swell, burst and absorb the liquid, thickening it into a sol (a colloidal solution, where tiny particles stay spread through the liquid).
On cooling, a concentrated starch mixture may set into a gel (a solid-like network that holds the liquid), which is why a cooled custard or sauce can become firm.
Gelatinised starch thickens white sauces, custard, soups, gravies, risotto and fillings for pies and flans.
To prevent lumps, the granules must be separated before they swell. Mix the starch with a little cold liquid first (a cornflour paste), or coat it in fat as in a roux.

A roux is a mixture of fat and flour cooked together before liquid is added. The fat separates the starch granules, and the starch in the flour gelatinises as the liquid is stirred in, giving a base for white sauce.
Starch is hygroscopic: it absorbs moisture from the air, so dry starchy foods such as flour, biscuits and crackers soften or clump if stored in damp air. Store them in airtight containers.
Sugar, especially brown sugar, is also hygroscopic, so it can turn hard or lumpy if left open in damp air.
notes.tip: Gelatinisation is starch plus liquid plus heat. For a culinary example, give a sauce, custard or soup, and say the granules swell, burst, absorb liquid and thicken into a sol. Hygroscopic means absorbs water from the air, not dissolves.

notes.h: Effects of dry and moist heat on carbohydrates in cooking
notes.b: How a carbohydrate food is cooked decides what happens to it. Dry heat browns it, while moist heat softens it and thickens liquids.
points: Dry heat (baking, roasting, toasting, grilling) on starch makes the granules burst and absorb fat, and dextrinisation occurs: the starch breaks down into brown dextrins. This gives a brown colour and a crisp, flavoursome crust on bread and toast.
Dry heat on sugar causes caramelisation and the Maillard reaction, which brown the surface of the food and give it flavour and a crisp texture.

Moist heat (boiling, steaming, stewing, poaching) on starch causes gelatinisation: the granules swell, burst and thicken the liquid, thickening sauces and puddings. Pasta, rice and potatoes become soft and digestible.
Moist heat softens the cellulose in vegetable cell walls, so vegetables become tender and easier to digest. The vegetable keeps its fibre.
Sugar dissolves in the cooking liquid and forms a syrup, for example when fruit is stewed, so the syrup carries the flavour of the fruit. Sugar also helps the fruit keep its shape.
notes.tip: For the effect of heat on starch, state which heat: dry heat gives brown dextrins and a crisp crust, while moist heat gives gelatinisation and a thickened liquid.

notes.h: Enzymes in the digestion of carbohydrates
notes.b: Enzymes (proteins that speed up chemical reactions) break complex carbohydrates down in stages until they are small enough to be absorbed.
points: 1. Salivary amylase in the mouth begins breaking starch down into smaller polysaccharides and maltose. This enzyme stops working in the stomach acid, so no carbohydrate digestion takes place in the stomach.
2. Pancreatic amylase, in pancreatic juice released into the small intestine, completes the breakdown of the remaining starch to maltose.

3. Maltase, sucrase and lactase, made by the wall of the small intestine and found in the intestinal juice, finish the job. Maltase splits maltose into two glucose units, sucrase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose, and lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose.
Only monosaccharides (single sugar units: glucose, fructose and galactose) are small enough to pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood.
Humans have no enzyme that digests cellulose, so it passes through the intestine as dietary fibre.
notes.tip: Know the enzyme that changes starch to maltose: salivary amylase in the mouth and amylase from the pancreas. Expect true or false statements such as starch is changed to maltose in the mouth (true) and carbohydrate digestion takes place in the stomach (false).

notes.b: Sugar does much more in the kitchen than sweeten. Each property has a use, and exam answers pair the two.
points: Sweetness: sweetens cakes, desserts and drinks. Solubility: dissolves to make syrups and icing and to bottle fruit.
Preservation: sugar draws water out of micro-organisms, so they cannot grow and spoilage is slowed in jam, jelly, chutney and crystallised fruit.
Fermentation: sugar is the food for yeast, which produces carbon dioxide that makes bread dough rise.
Aeration (trapping air): creamed sugar and fat trap air in cake mixtures such as sponge cakes. Whisking traps air in egg white, and the dissolved sugar keeps the foam stable, which makes meringue.

Maillard reaction: sugar reacts with amino acids (the units that make up protein) when heated, a non-enzymic browning that gives brown colour and flavour to roast meat, toast, roast potatoes and baked goods. Caramelisation is different because it involves sugar alone.
Gel formation: sugar, acid and pectin together set jam into a gel.
Caramelisation gives crème caramel and toffee, crystallisation gives confectionery, and inversion is used in jam and boiled sweets.
notes.tip: When asked for three properties of sugar, name each property, say what it is or what happens, and give one culinary use. Do not say that sugar denatures egg protein: whisking traps air, and the sugar stabilises the foam.

notes.h: The three browning reactions side by side
notes.b: Caramelisation, the Maillard reaction and dextrinisation all brown food, so they are easy to confuse. What differs is what is being heated and with what.
points: Caramelisation is sugar alone, heated dry until it melts and browns, so it needs no protein, as in caramel sauce.
The Maillard reaction needs sugar and amino acids together, heated dry, so it browns foods that contain both, such as toast and roast meat.
Dextrinisation is starch, not sugar, broken into brown dextrins by dry heat, which is why toast browns even though bread is mostly starch.
Gelatinisation is a different change again: starch heated in a liquid (moist heat) swells and thickens it, while inversion is the hydrolysis of sucrose by acid or enzyme.
notes.tip: Examiners expect these terms kept apart. Say what is heated (sugar, sugar with amino acids, or starch) and whether the heat is dry or moist.

notes.b: Hydrolysis is the reaction that splits big sugars into small ones, and it is the same reaction that happens in digestion. Inversion is the form of it that cooks use on sucrose.
points: Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a compound by reaction with water: the bond between two units is split and water is added across it. It is the reverse of condensation (joining units with the loss of water).

A disaccharide reacts with water, with enzymes or with heat and acid, and splits into its monosaccharide units. Sucrose gives glucose and fructose, lactose gives glucose and galactose, and maltose gives two glucose units.
Inversion is the hydrolysis of sucrose by heating with an acid (lemon juice, cream of tartar) or by the enzyme invertase. It produces invert sugar, a mixture of glucose and fructose.
Invert sugar is sweeter than sucrose (it contains fructose), is more soluble and is less likely to crystallise than sucrose.
This is why invert sugar is used in jam and boiled sweets, and for smooth icing and fondant. Honey and golden syrup contain invert sugar.
notes.tip: For hydrolysis and inversion, define hydrolysis as splitting with water, then say inversion is sucrose with acid or an enzyme giving invert sugar, with jam and boiled sweets as the uses.

notes.h: Caramelisation, crystallisation and dextrinisation (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Heating and cooling sugar and starch changes their colour, flavour and texture in three different ways. Each is wanted in some foods and avoided in others.
points: Caramelisation: sugar heated strongly on its own melts, turns from colourless to golden and then brown, producing caramel with a distinctive, pleasant flavour. Overheating makes it dark and bitter and finally burnt (carbonisation).
Caramel is used in caramel sauce, crème caramel, toffee and brûlée.
Crystallisation: when more sugar is dissolved than the liquid can hold at that temperature (a saturated solution) and the mixture cools, sugar crystals form.
Controlled crystallisation gives the texture of fudge, fondant and sweets, while unwanted large crystals make jam grainy.
Crystallisation is prevented by adding acid or glucose syrup (which causes inversion) and by not stirring while the sugar dissolves.
Dextrinisation: dry heat breaks starch down into shorter chains of glucose units called dextrins, which are brown. The 2005 scheme names the brown compound pyrodextrin.
Dextrinisation gives toast and the crust of baked bread their brown colour and flavour. Browned flour used for a roux thickens less, because its starch has already been broken into shorter chains.
Dextrinisation is a property of starch, not sugar.
notes.tip: For caramelisation and crystallisation, say that sugar melts and browns into caramel (excess gives bitterness), and that crystals form from a concentrated solution as it cools, wanted in fudge but unwanted in jam. For dextrinisation, say dry heat turns starch into brown dextrins, as in toast.

notes.h: Pectin extraction and gel formation (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Jam sets because of pectin, a substance in fruit cell walls. Making jam depends on getting the pectin out of the fruit and then giving it the right conditions to set.
points: Pectin is extracted by simmering the chopped fruit in water until soft. Acid, such as lemon juice, helps release the pectin from the cell walls.
Fruit high in pectin includes cooking apples and crab apples, citrus fruit (especially the peel), gooseberries, redcurrants and blackcurrants. Strawberries are low in pectin.
Unripe fruit contains more pectin than ripe fruit, so under-ripe apples are a good source of pectin for jam.
A gel forms only when pectin, sugar and acid are present in the right proportions and the mixture is boiled and then cooled.
During cooling, the pectin molecules link into a network that traps the sugar solution (the liquid), so the jam sets.
Too little pectin, as in strawberries, gives a runny jam. Add lemon juice or a pectin-rich fruit to fix this.
Pectin test (optional): a little cooled pectin extract added to methylated spirits (alcohol) forms a jelly-like clot if much pectin is present.
notes.tip: Name all three things a pectin gel needs (pectin, sugar and acid) and say that the pectin forms a network that traps the liquid.

notes.b: This simple test shows that starch does not thicken a cold liquid but does thicken it when heated.
points: Aim: to show the effect of heat on starch mixed with a liquid.
Method: mix a spoonful of cornflour with cold water and observe that it does not dissolve and does not thicken. Then heat the mixture while stirring and observe that it thickens.
Variable: temperature is the variable that changes (cold, then heated).
Control and comparison: the unheated cornflour and cold water mixture is compared with the heated one.
Result: cold, the starch settles as a cloudy suspension and the mixture stays thin; heated, the granules swell, burst and absorb the water, and the mixture thickens into a sol.
notes.tip: Label every investigation with its aim, method, control and result.

notes.h: Investigation: caramelisation of sugar (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Heating sugar on its own, with no water, shows caramelisation happening step by step.
points: Aim: to observe how granulated sugar changes when it is heated on its own, with no water added.
Method: place a measured quantity of granulated sugar in a dry, heavy-based pan on a low heat, stirring gently as it melts, and note the colour and smell at regular intervals.
Variables: heating time is the independent variable; colour, smell and taste are the dependent variables.
Control: a sample of the same sugar left unheated, for comparison.
Safety: molten sugar is extremely hot and causes severe burns, so use heatproof utensils and keep hands and skin away from the pan.
Expected results: the colour darkens gradually from pale to golden, then deep brown, and the caramel smell strengthens.
notes.tip: Label every investigation with its aim, method, control and result.

notes.h: Investigations: dextrinisation and inversion (Higher Level only)
notes.b: These two tests show a change in starch caused by dry heat and a change in sucrose caused by acid.
points: Dextrinisation, aim: to show that dry heat changes starch. Method: toast white bread, or brown flour in a dry pan, or compare a roux cooked for different times.
Dextrinisation, result: the browned starch is darker and thickens less than unbrowned starch, because its chains are shorter. Safety: the pan is hot.
Inversion, aim: to show that acid changes sucrose. Method: boil a sucrose solution with a little lemon juice and cool it.
Inversion, result: the invert sugar does not crystallise as readily and is sweeter.
A Benedict's test shows the invert sugar: reducing sugars give an orange-red colour, while sucrose does not.
notes.tip: Label every investigation with its aim, method, control and result.

keyTerms.definition: The breakdown of a compound by reaction with water, which splits the bond between its units.
The hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose, caused by heating with an acid or by the enzyme invertase.
The mixture of glucose and fructose produced when sucrose is inverted, which resists crystallisation.
The browning of sugar when it is heated alone, producing caramel with a distinctive flavour.
The formation of sugar crystals from a concentrated sugar solution as it cools.
The formation of brown dextrins from starch when dry heat is applied.
The swelling and bursting of starch granules in a heated liquid, which thickens the liquid into a sol.
Describes a substance that absorbs moisture from the air, as starch and sugar do.
A polysaccharide in fruit that forms a gel with sugar and acid.
The browning and flavour development that occurs when sugar and amino acids react under dry heat.

Monosaccharides formed when sucrose is inverted

factCards.definition: Gelatinisation of starch, which thickens liquids, and softening of cellulose in vegetable cell walls.

factCards.definition: The glycosidic link, formed by a condensation reaction that releases water.

questions.prompt: Describe two properties of sugar that are useful in cooking, giving a culinary example of each.
questions.model: Caramelisation: heated sugar melts and browns to caramel, used in crème caramel or caramel sauce. Crystallisation: sugar crystals form from a concentrated solution as it cools, used in fudge or fondant. Other acceptable properties: solubility (syrups for icing), Maillard browning (roasted meat), aeration (sponge cakes), preservation (jam), fermentation (bread).

questions.prompt: Explain how dry heat and moist heat change carbohydrates during cooking, and describe how enzymes break down carbohydrates during digestion.
questions.model: Dry heat: starch is converted to brown dextrins (dextrinisation), giving toast and baked bread a brown colour; sugar caramelises and reacts with amino acids in the Maillard reaction, browning and flavouring roasted foods. Moist heat: starch granules swell, burst and absorb liquid (gelatinisation), thickening sauces, custard and soup; cellulose in vegetable cell walls softens so vegetables become tender. Digestion: salivary amylase in the mouth and pancreatic amylase in the small intestine break starch down to maltose; maltase, sucrase and lactase split maltose, sucrose and lactose into monosaccharides, which are absorbed into the blood; cellulose is not broken down and passes through as fibre.
